story: Gros Morne is famous for its rocks. The Tablelands, in the south of the park, are a slab of the Earth's mantle, formed far below the ocean floor and thrust up about half a billion years ago when ancient continents collided to build the Appalachian chain. Their peridotite is rich in magnesium and iron and poor in the nutrients most plants need, so the mountain stands bare and orange among green hills: one of the few places on Earth where a complete cross-section of ocean crust and mantle lies exposed.

At Green Point, layers laid down on an ancient sea floor almost 500 million years ago mark the boundary between the Cambrian and Ordovician periods; the cliff is the world's reference section for the base of the Ordovician. Inland, the Long Range Mountains rise abruptly from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to a plateau more than 800 metres high, cut by glaciers into deep troughs. Western Brook Pond is one, a landlocked fjord between cliffs of 1.25-billion-year-old rock, the oldest in the park. UNESCO inscribed Gros Morne in 1987 for this record of the Earth's evolution and for its beauty.

The plateau is a slice of arctic tundra far south of its usual range, with rare alpine plants, some of the most southerly rock ptarmigan and Arctic hare, and calving grounds for woodland caribou. Newfoundland has only fourteen native mammals, and moose are not one of them: introduced more than a century ago and without predators, they reached 7,800 in the park by 1995 and kept the balsam fir forest from growing back. The park now manages their numbers, and the forest is recovering. Atlantic salmon returns in Western Brook have climbed from fewer than 30 in the mid-1980s to between 500 and 1,000.

People have lived here for at least 4,500 years: Maritime Archaic peoples first, then Groswater and Dorset peoples from the eastern Arctic, and from about 2,000 years ago cultures that included the ancestors of the Beothuk. The Mi'kmaq count the island as part of their traditional nation. The Norse sailed this coast around AD 1000, Basques fished it in the 16th century and a French migratory cod fishery worked it from about 1600 until 1904. Settlement began in the early 1800s with a trading post in Bonne Bay. Eight communities, home to about 3,300 people, sit alongside the park, which was established in 1973.
howItWorks: Gros Morne is run by Parks Canada, and every visitor needs a park pass valid for the whole stay; youth 17 and under enter free. Daily admission is $12.25 for an adult, less from 1 November to 15 May, and the park sells its own calendar-year pass. It also accepts the Parks Canada Discovery Pass, which covers more than 80 Parks Canada places for 12 months and was listed in November 2026 at $83.50 for an adult, $71.50 for a senior and $167.50 for a family or group of up to seven in one vehicle. Passes are sold at the Visitor Centre, the Discovery Centre, the Wiltondale kiosk in summer and shops in nearby communities. Under the Canada Strong Pass, admission was free from 19 June to 7 September 2026; regular fees resumed on 8 September.

Campsites, oTENTiks, cabins, primitive campsites and the backcountry traverses are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service, online at reservation.pc.gc.ca or on 1-877-737-3783; bookings for the 2027 season open on 11 February 2027 at 8:30 am Newfoundland time. Every overnight trip away from a campground needs a permit as well as a park pass; primitive camping permits must be picked up before 4 pm at the Visitor Centre, the Discovery Centre or a campground kiosk, and you report to a park facility when you are back. The Long Range and Northern Traverses cross the plateau on routes with no trails, signs or markers; they are open only by reservation, the park caps the number of hikers on the Long Range each day, and every party must be able to navigate by map, compass and GPS.

The park's communities are not part of it, and some activities unusual in a national park are allowed under permit: eligible residents may harvest domestic timber from 15 October to 30 April, and snowmobiles may run with a permit on top of a park pass. Anglers need a Gros Morne trout or salmon permit. Motorboats are banned except on Trout River Pond and Deer Arm Pond, with motors under 10 hp, and off-road vehicles everywhere. Drones are prohibited, dogs must be leashed, and it is an offence to feed or harass wildlife or to take plants, rocks, fossils or antlers.

sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-western-brook-pond: A landlocked fjord between cliffs rising to 670 metres above sea level, with waterfalls spilling from the plateau. A 3-kilometre trail leads to the dock for a two-hour boat tour.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-the-tablelands: A barren orange mountain of the Earth's mantle. An easy 4-kilometre return trail runs along its base to Winter House Brook Canyon; Parks Canada leads two-hour guided walks.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-gros-morne-mountain: The park's highest point, 806 metres. A difficult 17-kilometre loop with 1,000 metres of climb crosses its arctic-alpine summit; closed 1 May to 27 June.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-green-point: Seaside cliffs of tilted sea-floor layers that mark the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary. Off Route 430, 500 metres north of the campground; best at low tide.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-lobster-cove-head-ligh: A century-old lighthouse above Bonne Bay with an exhibit on lightkeepers and local history, short headland trails, tide pools and a favourite spot for sunsets.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-broom-point-fishing-pr: The restored summer fishing station where three Mudge brothers and their families fished from 1941 to 1975. Grounds open year-round; buildings when staff are present.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-trout-river-pond: A pond below the Tablelands, with a trail along its shore into their heart. One of only two ponds in the park where small motorboats are allowed.
sightNotes.poi-ca-gros-morne-green-gardens: A 4.5-kilometre trail across the Tablelands and down to a volcanic coastline, with a small primitive campsite on the cliff top.

Primitive campsites at Stanleyville, Green Gardens, Ferry Gulch and Snug Harbour, with pit toilets; no campfires

chronology.text: Maritime Archaic peoples are living in the Gros Morne region, the earliest known of its inhabitants.
The Norse sail these waters for a short time.
Basque fishers work the coast, followed by a French migratory cod fishery that lasts from about 1600 until 1904.
A Dorset firm sets up a trading post in Bonne Bay, and permanent settlement begins.
The Mudge brothers begin fishing from Broom Point each summer, which they do until 1975.
Gros Morne National Park is established under a federal–provincial agreement.
UNESCO inscribes Gros Morne on the World Heritage List for its geology and natural beauty.
Introduced moose in the park reach a peak of 7,800; active management later brings the forest back.

safety: Weather on the Long Range plateau is harsher and less predictable than on the coast, and hypothermia is a real risk on backcountry trips. Carry warm, waterproof clothing in every season.

Gros Morne Mountain's summit trail is difficult: 17 kilometres, 1,000 metres of climb and six to eight and a half hours at least. Walk the loop clockwise so you climb the scree gully rather than descend it, and do not start when the summit is in cloud.
The traverses have no trails or markers, and low cloud can hide the way. Go only if someone in your party is confident navigating by map, compass and GPS.
Black bears live throughout the park. Keep a clean camp and use the food lockers; if you meet a bear, stay calm, do not run, and back away slowly while speaking softly.
Cell coverage is unreliable. In an emergency, call Parks Canada dispatch on 1-877-852-3100.
regulations: Every visitor needs a valid park pass for the whole stay; youth 17 and under enter free.
Drones and off-road vehicles are prohibited; motorboats are allowed only on Trout River Pond and Deer Arm Pond, with motors under 10 hp.
Camp only in designated campgrounds and sites, never at roadside pull-outs, trailheads or day-use areas. Fires only in proper fire boxes, using firewood the park provides.
Dogs must be on a leash at all times. Feeding, enticing or harassing wildlife is illegal, and pursuing animals with a camera counts as harassment.
Leave plants, rocks, fossils and antlers where you find them.

weather: The weather is unpredictable, and the coast and the Long Range Mountains can feel like different places. Spring comes late, and many trails keep snow well into May. July and August are the warmest and driest months, with daytime temperatures of about 16–25 °C, cooler nights and rain on average every second day; the heights are colder, especially in wind. September and early October are often pleasant, though snow can reach the high ground by late September. Winters run from about −10 to 0 °C with 4 to 4.5 metres of snow, and up to 10 metres on the heights; January to March is the season for cross-country skiing.
directions: Gros Morne is on the west coast of the island of Newfoundland. Deer Lake Regional Airport, 35 kilometres from the southern boundary, has direct flights from Halifax, Toronto, St. John's and, from May to October, Montreal, with car rental and buses on to the park. From the mainland, Marine Atlantic's year-round ferry runs from North Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Port aux Basques in about six hours; book ahead. From there it is 300 kilometres, about four hours, to the park. Route 430, the only road up the Northern Peninsula, runs through the park, and Route 431 leads to Woody Point and Trout River.
